Laws concerning servants (verses 1–11)

The laws in this chapter help explain the fifth and sixth commandments.

They reflect a society and customs very different from ours, and Henry says they are not binding on us as civil laws.

Nevertheless, they explain the enduring moral law and the basic principles of justice.

A person held in servitude pictured humanity's bondage to sin, Satan and the condemnation of the law.

People fell into this bondage when they robbed God of his glory by breaking his commands.

In the servant's release, we see a picture of the freedom Christ gives his people.

Christ, the Son of God, sets them free from slavery so that they become truly free.

That liberty is given freely, without money or payment, entirely through grace.

Laws protecting life and restraining violence (verses 12–21)

God gives and sustains life through his providence.

Through his law he also protects it.

A deliberate murderer was to be taken even from God's altar for judgment.

But God provided cities of refuge for people who caused another person's death without intending any harm.

They had not committed deliberate murder, but had caused an accidental death while doing something lawful.

Children should hear the solemn judgment God's word pronounces upon ingratitude and disobedience toward parents.

If they have cursed a parent—even secretly in their hearts—or struck a parent, they should remember that God will hold them accountable unless they repent and flee to the Savior for refuge.

Parents, meanwhile, should raise their children carefully.

They should give them a good example, particularly in controlling their own tempers and praying for them.

They must take care not to provoke their children to anger.

In times of poverty, Israelites sometimes sold their own labor or that of their children.

Magistrates could sell some offenders as punishment, and creditors were sometimes allowed to sell people who could not pay what they owed.

But kidnapping people for the purpose of enslaving them is classed in the New Testament among the gravest crimes.

These laws also required compensation when someone was injured, even if the injury did not lead to death.

The gospel instructs masters to restrain their threats (Ephesians 6:9).

They should remember Job's question: What will I do when God rises to judge me? (Job 31:13–14).

Further principles of justice (verses 22–36)

The cases in this passage give rules of justice for the society of Israel.

Their principles still help us judge similar situations.

They teach us to take great care not to wrong another person, whether directly or indirectly.

When we have caused a loss, we should be ready to make it good.

Indeed, we should desire that no one suffer loss because of what we have done.

Verses 1-11
The laws in this chapter relate to the fifth and sixth commandments; and though they differ from our times and customs, nor are they binding on us, yet they explain the moral law, and the rules of natural justice. The servant, in the state of servitude, was an emblem of that state of bondage to sin, Satan, and the law, which man is brought into by robbing God of his glory, by the transgression of his precepts. Likewise in being made free, he was an emblem of that liberty wherewith Christ, the Son of God, makes free from bondage his people, who are free indeed; and made so freely, without money and without price, of free grace.
[Exod.21.12-Exod.21.21]
Verses 12-21
God, who by his providence gives and maintains life, by his law protects it. A wilful murderer shall be taken even from God's altar. But God provided cities of refuge to protect those whose unhappiness it was, and not their fault, to cause the death of another; for such as by accident, when a man is doing a lawful act, without intent of hurt, happens to kill another. Let children hear the sentence of God's word upon the ungrateful and disobedient; and remember that God will certainly requite it, if they have ever cursed their parents, even in their hearts, or have lifted up their hands against them, except they repent, and flee for refuge to the Saviour. And let parents hence learn to be very careful in training up their children, setting them a good example, especially in the government of their passions, and in praying for them; taking heed not to provoke them to wrath. Through poverty the Israelites sometimes sold themselves or their children; magistrates sold some persons for their crimes, and creditors were in some cases allowed to sell their debtors who could not pay. But "man-stealing," the object of which is to force another into slavery, is ranked in the New Testament with the greatest crimes. Care is here taken, that satisfaction be made for hurt done to a person, though death do not follow. The gospel teaches masters to forbear, and to moderate threatenings, [Eph.6.9] Ep 6:9, considering with Job, What shall I do, when God riseth up? [Job.31.13] Job 31:13, [Job.31.14] 14.
[Exod.21.22-Exod.21.36]
Verses 22-36
The cases here mentioned give rules of justice then, and still in use, for deciding similar matters. We are taught by these laws, that we must be very careful to do no wrong, either directly or indirectly. If we have done wrong, we must be very willing to make it good, and be desirous that nobody may lose by us.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Judicial laws.

The spirit of these laws

God's people should always be ready to show gentleness and mercy, according to the spirit of the laws given here.

We must answer to God not only for the wrong we do deliberately, out of malice, but also for harm caused by our carelessness.

Therefore, whenever we have harmed our neighbor, we should make restitution, even when no human law forces us to do so.

Let these Scriptures remind us what God's grace does in those to whom it has truly appeared.

Grace teaches us and, by its holy power, enables us to turn away from ungodliness and worldly desires.

It teaches us to live with self-control, righteousness and devotion to God in this present world (Titus 2:12).

God's grace also teaches us that the Lord himself is our portion.

In him there is more than enough to satisfy every desire of our souls.

Laws against falsehood and injustice (verses 1–9)

The law of Moses bears clear marks of sound moral judgment and wise government.

All its provisions serve its stated purposes: Israel was to worship the one true God and remain distinct from the pagan nations around it.

We must never allow partisan loyalties, friends, witnesses or popular opinions to distort our judgments.

They must not lead us to minimize serious wrongs or exaggerate minor ones.

They must not cause us to excuse guilty people, accuse innocent people or misrepresent the facts in any way.

The seventh-year rest, Sabbath, and festivals (verses 10–19)

Every seventh year, Israel's land was to rest.

The people were not to plow or sow it.

They could eat what grew on its own, but were not to collect it for storage.

Henry understands this law as teaching dependence on God's providence.

It also taught Israel to trust God's faithfulness in providing greater harvests while they followed his appointed seasons.

The rest of the land pictured the heavenly rest.

In that rest, the labors, worries and concerns of this world will end forever.

Israel was strictly forbidden to honor the gods of the surrounding nations.

The people were particularly inclined toward idolatry, so they were to erase even the remembrance of those false gods.

God also required his people to gather solemnly in worship at the place he would choose.

They were to come together before the Lord.

What a good Master we serve!

He has made rejoicing before him one of our duties.

We should gladly devote to his service the portion of time he requires.

His Sabbaths and appointed acts of worship should be feasts to our souls.

The Israelites were not to come before God empty-handed.

Likewise, we should never approach his worship empty-hearted.

Our hearts should be filled with holy longing for him and renewed dedication to his service.

God takes pleasure in spiritual sacrifices of this kind.

God promises to guide Israel to Canaan (verses 20–33)

God promised to guide and protect Israel throughout the wilderness journey and bring the people into the promised land.

He said that he would send his angel before them.

With this promise came a command: they must obey the angel God would send.

Christ is the Angel of Jehovah, Henry says, as the apostle teaches in 1 Corinthians 10:9.

God also promised Israel a secure and pleasant settlement in Canaan.

The condition was entirely reasonable.

They were to serve only the true God, not the gods of the nations—gods that were no gods at all.

Consider how generous God's promises were.

He promised good food, continuing health, growing possessions and long life.

In this way, godliness has a promise for the present life as well.

He also promised victory over their enemies.

God sent swarms of hornets ahead of Israel's armies.

He can use even such small creatures to judge the enemies of his people.

In kindness toward the church, God often defeats its enemies little by little.

That keeps us watchful and continually dependent on him.

In the same way, sinful habits and desires are driven from believers' hearts gradually, not all at once.

Alongside the promises came another command: Israel must not make alliances of friendship with idolaters.

Anyone who wants to avoid evil practices must also avoid company that draws them into evil.

Living among people devoted to wrongdoing can be dangerous.

Other people's sins may become traps for us.

Our greatest danger comes from people who lead us to sin against God.

Verses 1-9
In the law of Moses are very plain marks of sound moral feeling, and of true political wisdom. Every thing in it is suited to the desired and avowed object, the worship of one only God, and the separation of Israel from the pagan world. Neither parties, friends, witnesses, nor common opinions, must move us to lessen great faults, to aggravate small ones, excuse offenders, accuse the innocent, or misrepresent any thing.
[Exod.23.10-Exod.23.19]
Verses 10-19
Every seventh year the land was to rest. They must not plough or sow it; what the earth produced of itself, should be eaten, and not laid up. This law seems to have been intended to teach dependence on Providence, and God's faithfulness in sending the larger increase while they kept his appointments. It was also typical of the heavenly rest, when all earthly labours, cares, and interests shall cease for ever. All respect to the gods of the heathen is strictly forbidden. Since idolatry was a sin to which the Israelites leaned, they must blot out the remembrance of the gods of the heathen. Solemn religious attendance on God, in the place which he should choose, is strictly required. They must come together before the Lord. What a good Master do we serve, who has made it our duty to rejoice before him! Let us devote with pleasure to the service of God that portion of our time which he requires, and count his sabbaths and ordinances to be a feast unto our souls. They were not to come empty-handed; so now, we must not come to worship God empty-hearted; our souls must be filled with holy desires toward him, and dedications of ourselves to him; for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.
[Exod.23.20-Exod.23.33]
Verses 20-33
It is here promised that they should be guided and kept in their way through the wilderness to the land of promise, Behold, I send an angel before thee, mine angel. The precept joined with this promise is, that they be obedient to this angel whom God would send before them. Christ is the Angel of Jehovah; this is plainly taught by St. Paul, [1Cor.10.9] 1Co 10:9. They should have a comfortable settlement in the land of Canaan. How reasonable are the conditions of this promise; that they should serve the only true God; not the gods of the nations, which are no gods at all. How rich are the particulars of this promise! The comfort of their food, the continuance of their health, the increase of their wealth, the prolonging their lives to old age. Thus hath godliness the promise of the life that now is. It is promised that they should subdue their enemies. Hosts of hornets made way for the hosts of Israel; such mean creatures can God use for chastising his people's enemies. In real kindness to the church, its enemies are subdued by little and little; thus we are kept on our guard, and in continual dependence on God. Corruptions are driven out of the hearts of God's people, not all at once, but by little and little. The precept with this promise is, that they should not make friendship with idolaters. Those that would keep from bad courses, must keep from bad company. It is dangerous to live in a bad neighbourhood; others' sins will be our snares. Our greatest danger is from those who would make us sin against God.

The covenant is confirmed with blood (verses 1–8)

God and Israel entered into a solemn covenant.

Its solemnity pointed toward the covenant of grace between God and believers through Jesus Christ.

As soon as God set Israel apart as his own people, he gave them his written word to govern their life.

He has continued to govern his people through his word ever since.

God's covenants and commands are just in themselves and intended for our good.

The more thoughtfully we consider them and the more fully and clearly they are explained, the more reason we see to accept them and obey.

Blood from the sacrifice was sprinkled on the altar, the book and the people.

Neither the people themselves, their moral obedience nor their religious services could be accepted by a holy God without the shedding and application of blood.

Every blessing God gave them was an act of mercy.

He intended to treat them kindly.

In the same way, a sinner who trusts in Christ's blood can offer obedience that is willing and acceptable to God.

The elders behold God's glory (verses 9–11)

Israel's elders saw the God of Israel.

They received a glimpse of his glory.

Whatever they saw could not be represented in an image or picture.

Yet they saw enough to know that God truly was with them.

Scripture describes only what was beneath his feet.

Sapphires formed the pavement under them.

May we also keep all the wealth of this world beneath our feet, rather than setting it in our hearts.

Believers now see the glorious justice and holiness of God much more clearly in the face of Jesus Christ than they saw them even through terrifying conviction of sin.

Through the Savior they can enjoy communion with the holy God.

Moses ascends into the cloud (verses 12–18)

A cloud covered the mountain for six days.

It was a sign of God's special presence there.

Moses trusted that the One who had called him upward would also keep him safe.

The very attributes of God that terrify the wicked are a cause of joy to believers who approach him with humble reverence.

Through faith in the atoning Sacrifice, we hope to receive an honor greater than anything Moses experienced on earth.

Now we see only dimly, as though through a mirror.

But when God appears, we will see him face to face.

That vision will not last for a few days.

It will continue throughout eternity, with joy that remains bright and may grow brighter still.

Offerings for God's dwelling among Israel (verses 1–9)

God had chosen Israel as his own special people, above all other nations.

He himself would be their King.

He therefore commanded that a royal dwelling be prepared for him among them.

This dwelling was called the sanctuary, the holy place, or the habitation.

There God would show his presence among his people.

Because Israel lived in tents during its journey through the wilderness, God's royal dwelling was to be a tabernacle—a tent that could travel with them.

The people were to supply the materials Moses needed, each person giving freely and willingly.

The best use we can make of earthly possessions is to honor God through acts of devotion and charity.

We should ask not only, “What must we do?” but also, “What can we do for God?”

Whatever we give him, we should give cheerfully, not resentfully.

God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).

We should consider money spent in his service well spent.

Yet everything done in God's service must also be done according to his directions.

The ark and the mercy seat (verses 10–22)

The ark was a chest covered in gold.

It was made to hold the two tablets of God's law.

Those tablets are called the testimony, because through them God testified to his will.

The law was a testimony for Israel, guiding the people in their duty.

If they disobeyed, it would also be a testimony against them.

The ark stood in the Most Holy Place.

The high priest sprinkled sacrificial blood and burned incense before it.

Above it appeared the visible glory that represented God's presence.

Henry sees the ark as a picture of Christ.

His human nature was without sin and did not undergo corruption.

It was personally united with his divine nature, and through his death he made atonement for our violations of God's law.

The golden cherubim faced each other, both looking down toward the ark.

They represented the angels' attendance upon the Redeemer, their readiness to carry out his will, their presence when the saints gather, and their desire to understand the mysteries of the gospel.

The ark was covered by a golden lid called the mercy seat.

God was said to dwell—or sit enthroned—between the cherubim above that mercy seat.

There, like a king seated on his throne, he gave his law and listened to those who came to him in prayer.

The table of the bread of the Presence (verses 23–30)

A wooden table covered with gold stood in the outer room of the tabernacle.

The bread of the Presence was always to be placed on it.

The table, its furnishings and their use seem to picture the fellowship the Lord enjoys with his redeemed people through his appointed means of worship.

They point to the provisions and feasts of his household.

They also picture the food believers find for their souls whenever they hunger for it.

Finally, they point to the delight God takes in his people's lives and service, which are presented before him in Christ.

The golden lampstand (verses 31–40)

The lampstand represented the light of God's word and Spirit, given through Jesus Christ to believers in this dark world.

That light guides their worship and obedience and brings them comfort.

Compared with the glory it will enjoy in heaven, the church is still in darkness, just as the tabernacle was.

Yet God's word shines like a lamp in a dark place (2 Peter 1:19).

How dark the world would be without it!

Verse 40 gives Moses an explicit warning.

Nothing was to be left to Moses' personal preference, to the workmen's creativity or to the people's wishes.

God's will had to be followed in every detail.

Christ likewise commanded his disciples to observe everything he had instructed them (Matthew 28:20).

Let us remember that believers themselves are temples of the Holy Spirit.

God's law is written on our hearts.

We should live in fellowship with him, enjoy the feast of his appointed ordinances, and be the light of the world—if we are truly following Christ.

May the Lord help us examine ourselves in the light of this description of faith and live accordingly.

The richly woven curtains (verses 1–6)

God made his presence known to Israel through a tabernacle, or tent, because that suited the people's life in the wilderness.

He adapts the signs of his favor and the gifts of his grace to the circumstances and needs of his people.

The inner curtains were to be richly made.

They were embroidered with cherubim.

Henry understands these figures as a reminder that God's angels camp around his church (Psalm 34:7).

The goats' hair curtains and coverings (verses 7–14)

The outer curtains were made of less valuable materials.

They were longer and wider than the inner ones, so that they covered them completely.

Other coverings of animal skins protected the whole structure.

Henry sees in these layers a picture of Christ's person and teaching, the church of true Christians, and heavenly realities.

Outwardly, these things may appear humble and unimpressive.

Inwardly, however, and in God's sight, they are glorious and precious.

The boards, bases and crossbars (verses 15–30)

Each silver base weighed about 115 pounds, according to Henry's reckoning.

The bases stood in rows upon the ground.

Strong boards of acacia wood, covered in gold, were fitted into pairs of bases by their joints.

Together they formed the walls along the two sides and the western end.

Bars passing through golden rings bound the walls together.

Curtains were then spread over the structure.

The tabernacle could be moved, yet it was solid and stable.

Its materials were also extremely costly.

In all this, Henry sees a picture of God's church.

It is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ himself as the chief cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20–21).

The veil of the Most Holy Place (verses 31–37)

A veil hung from pillars and divided the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.

It prevented people from looking into the innermost sanctuary.

The apostle explains its meaning in Hebrews 9:8.

The ceremonial law could not make worshipers perfect.

Simply observing its ordinances could not bring anyone into heaven.

The way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been fully revealed while the first tabernacle still stood.

Life and immortality remained hidden until the gospel brought them to light.

The tearing of the veil when Christ died pointed to that new revelation (Matthew 27:51).

Through Jesus' blood we now have freedom to enter the Most Holy Place in our worship.

But that access never removes our duty to approach God with holy reverence.

Another curtain hung at the outer entrance of the tabernacle.

That curtain was the only outward protection the sanctuary had.

God himself takes care of his church on earth.

If he chooses, a curtain can defend his house as effectively as bronze gates and iron bars.

With these pictures of Christ and his church before us, what judgment do we make of them?

Do we see glory in Christ's person?

Do we recognize excellence in his character, something precious in his salvation, and wisdom in the teaching of the cross?

Can our religion stand examination?

Are we more concerned to have hearts approved by God than reputations admired by other people?

The sockets of silver each weighed about 115 pounds; they were placed in rows on the ground. In every pair of these sockets, a strong board of shittim-wood, covered with plates of gold, was fitted by mortises and tenons. Thus walls were formed for the two sides, and for the west end. The wall was further held together by bars, which passed through rings of gold. Over this the curtains were spread. Though movable, it was strong and firm. The materials were very costly. In all this it was a type of the church of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief Corner-stone, [Eph.2.20] Ep 2:20, 21.

This vail was for a partition between the holy place and the most holy; which forbade any to look into the holiest of all. The apostle tells what was the meaning of this vail, [Heb.9.8] He 9:8. That the ceremonial law could not make the comers thereunto perfect, nor would the observance of it bring men to heaven; the way into the holiest of all was not made manifest, while the first tabernacle was standing. Life and immortality lay hidden till they were brought to light by the gospel; which was signified by the rending of this vail at the death of Christ, [Matt.27.51] Mt 27:51. With this typical description of Christ and his church before us, what is our judgment of these matters? Do we see any glory in the person of Christ? any excellence in his character? any thing precious in his salvation? or any wisdom in the doctrine of the cross? Will our religion bear examination? and are we more careful to approve our hearts to God than our characters toward men?

The altar stood in the court in front of the tabernacle.

Aaron and his sons are appointed as priests (verses 1–5)

Until this time, the heads of households had served as priests and offered sacrifices.

Now the office was restricted to Aaron's family, and that arrangement continued until the coming of the gospel.

The priests' special clothing distinguished them from the people.

But it also represented the holy conduct that should be the glory and beauty of everyone who ministers in God's name.

Without such a life, both the minister and the ministry will be despised.

These garments also pointed to the glory of divine majesty and the beauty of perfect holiness.

Those qualities make Jesus Christ our great High Priest.

Under the gospel, our own adornment should not consist chiefly of gold and costly clothing.

It should be the garments of salvation and the robe of righteousness.

The ephod (verses 6–14)

The high priest wore a richly made ephod as his outer garment.

Other priests wore plain linen ephods.

The high priest's ephod was a short sleeveless garment, fastened closely around the body with a belt.

Its shoulder pieces joined together by precious stones set in gold.

One stone was placed on each shoulder, engraved with the names of Israel's children.

This pictured Christ, our High Priest, who carries his people before the Lord as a continual memorial.

Henry compares the ephod with Christ's seamless coat, woven in one piece from the top.

He also speaks of the golden bells associated with this garment: their value and pleasant sound represent the good profession believers make.

The pomegranates represent the good fruit they bear.

The breastplate; the Urim and Thummim (verses 15–30)

The high priest's finest ornament was his breastplate, a beautifully worked piece of cloth.

Each tribe's name was engraved upon a precious stone set into it.

These stones showed how precious and honorable God's people are in his sight.

Even the smallest and poorest tribe was represented by a jewel on the high priest's breast.

Likewise, every believer is dear to Christ, no matter how little other people value that believer.

The priest carried the tribes' names on both his shoulders and his breast.

This reminds us of the strength and love with which Jesus intercedes for his own.

He carries them with almighty power and holds them close with tender affection.

What comfort this gives us whenever we approach God!

The Urim and Thummim were placed in the breastplate.

Through them, God's will was made known in difficult or doubtful matters.

Their names mean light and integrity, Henry explains.

Many different ideas have been proposed about what they actually were.

He considers it most likely that they were the twelve precious stones in the breastplate.

But Christ is now our divine Oracle.

In these last days, God reveals himself and his will to us through his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2; John 1:18).

Christ is the true Light, the faithful Witness and the Truth itself.

From him we receive the Spirit of Truth, who guides us into all truth.

The robe and the golden plate (verses 31–39)

The robe worn beneath the ephod reached to the knees and had no sleeves.

Aaron had to minister in the garments God appointed.

We must serve the Lord with holy fear, remembering that in ourselves we deserve death.

A golden plate was fastened to Aaron's forehead.

On it were engraved the words “Holiness to the Lord.”

This reminded him that God is holy and that priests must be holy and wholly dedicated to him.

The declaration appeared openly on Aaron's forehead.

In the same way, our belonging to God should be openly professed.

The letters were engraved like those on a seal.

They were meant to be deep and lasting—not merely painted on, to be washed away.

Our holiness to the Lord must be just as durable and real.

Christ is our High Priest.

Through him our sins are forgiven and no longer counted against us.

Only because of Christ are our persons and actions pleasing to God.

Clothing for Aaron's sons (verses 40–43)

The priests' garments pointed to the righteousness of Christ.

Without that righteousness, we will appear before God bearing our own guilt and will die.

Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments (Revelation 16:15).

And blessed be God that he has given us a High Priest of his own choosing.

Christ has been appointed and set apart for his work.

The glory of his divine majesty and the beauty of his perfect holiness equip him fully for his great office.

Happy are we if the spiritual meaning of the law teaches us how perfectly suited he is to our need.

We cannot approach a holy God or find acceptance except through him.

We receive no light, wisdom or perfection apart from Christ.

We possess no true beauty or glory except through becoming like him.

Let us take courage from our High Priest's power, love and compassion.

We may come boldly to the throne of grace, where we will receive mercy and find grace for the help we need.

Happy are we, if by the law spiritually understood, we see that such a High Priest became us; that we cannot draw near to a holy God, or be accepted, but by him. There is no light, no wisdom, no perfection, but from him; no glory, no beauty, but in being like unto him. Let us take encouragement from the power, love, and compassion of our High Priest, to draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.

Aaron and his sons are consecrated (verses 1–37)

Aaron and his sons were to be set apart for the priestly office through solemn ceremonies.

Our Lord Jesus is the great High Priest whom we profess.

God appointed him to this work.

He was anointed with the Spirit, and so bears the title Messiah, or Christ.

He is clothed with glory and beauty.

He was sanctified through his own blood and made perfect—or fully consecrated to his mission—through sufferings (Hebrews 2:10).

All believers are also spiritual priests.

They offer spiritual sacrifices to God (1 Peter 2:5).

Washed in Christ's blood, they have been made priests to God (Revelation 1:5–6).

They too are clothed with the beauty of holiness and have received an anointing (1 John 2:27).

The Spirit of God is called the finger of God.

Compare Luke 11:20 with Matthew 12:28.

Through that Spirit, the merit of Christ is applied to our souls.

The priests' consecration therefore represents the admission of a sinner into the spiritual priesthood.

That person may now offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

The continual sacrifices and God's presence (verses 38–46)

One lamb was to be offered on the altar each morning, and another each evening.

These sacrifices pointed to Christ's continual intercession for his church.

He offered himself once for all.

Yet the benefits of that one sacrifice continue, as he lives forever to intercede.

The morning and evening lambs also teach us to present our own daily spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise to God.

Morning and evening worship are among the most necessary duties of each day.

They are also among the greatest comforts available to us.

We should observe prayer times as faithfully as meal times.

Those who do not keep coming to God's throne of grace starve their own souls.

Steadiness in serving God brings the comfort of fellowship with him.

The altar of incense (verses 1–10)

The incense altar represented the Son of God in his human nature.

The incense burning upon it pictured his pleading on behalf of his people.

Its daily offering, morning and evening, represented Christ's continual intercession.

Once each year, the blood of atonement was applied to the altar.

This taught that Christ's intercession draws all its power from the suffering he endured on earth.

We need no sacrifice or intercessor apart from Christ himself.

The ransom payment (verses 11–16)

The required contribution was half a shekel.

Henry compares this with about fifteen pence in the money of his own time.

The rich must not give more, and the poor must not give less.

The souls of rich and poor are equally precious.

God shows no favoritism (Acts 10:34; Job 34:19).

In other offerings, people gave in proportion to their financial means.

But this contribution represented the ransom of the soul and therefore had to be the same for everyone.

Every soul is of equal value.

All face the same danger, and all need a ransom.

The money collected supported the service of the tabernacle.

Those who benefit from public worship should not resent the expense of maintaining it.

Money cannot atone for anyone's soul.

But it can be used to honor the One who has made atonement and to support the proclamation of the gospel through which its benefits are applied.

The bronze basin for washing (verses 17–21)

A large bronze basin filled with water stood near the tabernacle entrance.

Aaron and his sons were required to wash their hands and feet there each time they entered to minister.

This taught them to serve God in purity and to dread the defilement of sin.

They were not merely to be washed once, when they first became priests.

They also had to wash repeatedly and remain clean whenever they came to serve.

We likewise need to come to God every day.

We must continually renew our repentance and look to Christ's blood for forgiveness.

We offend against God in many ways each day.

The holy oil and incense (verses 22–38)

God gave exact instructions for preparing the oil for anointing and the incense used in the tabernacle.

The fragrant oil, pleasing to the eye and to the sense of smell, pictured the excellence of holiness.

Christ's name is like perfume poured out (Song of Songs 1:3).

And the good name of a Christian is like precious ointment (Ecclesiastes 7:1).

The incense offered on the golden altar was made from sweet spices.

Before use it had to be crushed very fine.

Henry sees this as a picture of the Redeemer's bruising in sacrifice, an offering with a sweet fragrance to God.

The same oil and incense must not be manufactured for ordinary private use.

God thereby taught the people to revere the worship appointed for him.

We must not treat as common or misuse anything through which God reveals himself.

It is a great insult to God to make jokes about sacred things or amuse ourselves at the expense of his word and ordinances.

It is especially dangerous—and may prove fatal—to use an outward profession of Christ's gospel as a means of advancing worldly interests.
